String diagrams for symmetric powers I: In symmetric monoidal ℚ ≥ 0 \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0} -linear categories The author would like to thank John Baez, Rick Blute, Vikraman Choudhury, Sacha Ikonicoff, Shin-ya Katsumata, JS Lemay, Phil Scott, Thomas Vandeven and Geoff Vooys for useful discussions and their support of this research project. For this research, the author was financially supported by the University of Ottawa and Aix-Marseille University.
Jean-Baptiste Vienney

Abstract
Symmetric powers are an important notion in mathematics, computer science and physics. In mathematics, they are used to build symmetric algebras, in computer science, to build free exponential modalities of linear logic and in physics, Fock spaces. We study symmetric powers through the lens of category theory. We focus here on the simpler case where nonnegative rational scalars are available ie. we study symmetric powers in symmetric monoidal ℚ ≥ 0 \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0} -linear categories. Among the developments, a main point is the introduction of the notion of binomial graded bimonoid and the associated string diagrams which characterize symmetric powers in this setting.



1
Introduction

Symmetric powers are a useful notion in mathematics, computer science and physics. In mathematics, the
n^{th}
symmetric power of a module
M
with coefficients in some commutative semi-ring
R
is given by quotienting the
n^{th}
tensor power
M^{\otimes n}
by the equalities
x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n}=x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)}
for any permutation
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
. If
M
is a free module with basis
x_{1},...,x_{p}
, then
S^{n}(M)
is isomorphic to the space
R_{n}[x_{1},...,x_{p}]
of homogeneous polynomials of degree
n
with coefficients in
R
and indeterminates
x_{1},...,x_{n}
ie. the polynomials which can be written as a sum of monomials of the form
r.x_{i_{1}}...x_{i_{n}}
where
1\leq i_{1},...,i_{n}\leq p
. If we define
S(M)=\underset{n\geq 0}{\bigoplus}S^{n}(M)
, we obtain the symmetric algebra of
M
which is isomorphic to the space
R[x_{1},...,x_{p}]
of all polynomials. There is also the notion of
n^{th}
divided power
[
43
,
32
,
14
,
15
]
. The
n^{th}
divided power
\Gamma^{n}(M)
of
M
is the subspace of
M^{\otimes n}
constituted by all the elements which are invariant under the action
\sigma.x_{1}\otimes...x_{n}=x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}
of the symmetric group. In general the
n^{th}
symmetric power and the
n^{th}
divided power are not isomorphic, however, it happens if
R
is a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-algebra, ie a commutative semi-ring such that there exists a semi-ring morphism from
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
to
R
(for instance a field of characteristic
0
).

In physics, where most of the time we work over a field of characteristic
0
, if
M
is the space of states of a boson (for instance a photon), then the
n^{th}
symmetric power is then the space of states of a pack of
n
indistinguishable bosons. The direct sum of all the
n^{th}
symmetric powers is then known as the (bosonic) Fock space
[
25
]
.

In computer science, linear logic
[
27
]
is the logic of symmetric monoidal categories
\mathcal{C}
equipped with an exponential modality
\oc
, which is an endofunctor of
\mathcal{C}
which is equipped with further structure and must verify some axioms, in particular, that for every object
A\in\mathcal{C}
,
\oc A
is a cocommutative coalgebra. Especially interesting is then the equalizer
\Gamma^{n}(A)
of all the permutations
\sigma:A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
, which corresponds to the
n^{th}
divided power in algebra but is named symmetric power in this context. By taking the coproduct of all the
\Gamma^{n}(A)
, or some variant, we can hope to obtain a canonical kind of exponential modality which is called a free exponential modality
[
42
]
.

Linear logic possesses several variants such as graded linear logic
[
28
,
13
,
26
,
24
,
11
,
33
]
and differential linear logic (
[
22
,
23
,
21
]
, see the bibliography of
[
21
]
for all the original references). In graded linear logic, we replace the exponential modality
\oc
with a graded exponential modality
(\oc_{r})_{r\in R}
where
R
is some ordered commutative semi-ring. In the simplest case, we can take
R=\mathbb{N}
equipped with the discrete order (ie.
n\leq p
if and only if
n=p
). A proof from
\oc_{n}A
to
B
must then be interpreted as a proof of
B
which uses exactly
n
times its argument
A
, or an algorithm which uses exactly
n
times its entry of type
A
to produce in output a result of type
B
. More broadly, we can interpret a proof from
\oc_{n}A
to
B
as any morphism from the object
\oc_{n}A
to the object
B
in an appropriate symmetric monoidal category. In linear logic, a proof from
\oc A
to
B
must be interpreted as an algorithm which uses as many times as desired its entry of type
A
to produce an output of type
B
and in differential linear logic, we can differentiate such an algorithm. Differential categories
[
9
,
8
]
are the categorical models of differential linear logic. In a differential category, a morphism from
\oc A
to
B
must be interpreted as a smooth differentiable function from
A
to
B
.

The author together with Lemay introduced the notions of graded differential linear logic and graded differential categories
[
38
]
which combine differential linear logic and graded linear logic or differential categories and the models of graded linear logic. Now a morphism from
\oc_{n}A
to
B
must be interpreted as a smooth function from
A
to
B
which possesses some degree
n
. When we differentiate it we obtain a morphism
\oc_{n-1}A\otimes A\rightarrow B
of degree
n-1
in its first entry and linear in its second entry. The main example of
\mathbb{N}
-graded differential category is a
\mathbb{N}
-graded codifferential category meaning that it is not the category
\mathcal{C}
but its opposite
\mathcal{C}^{op}
which is a
\mathbb{N}
-graded differential category. And it is obtained by taking
\oc_{n}A
equal to the
n^{th}
symmetric power (in the sense of algebra) ie. the coequalizer of all the permutations
A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
in some monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
enriched over commutative monoids. Write
S^{n}A
for this object, what we can differentiate are now morphisms from
B
to
S^{n}A
which can be interpreted as a list of homogeneous polynomials of degree
n
with indeterminates in
A
. In a category of modules, if
A
is a free module, then the indeterminates are given by a basis of
A
. In the category
\mathbf{Rel}
of sets and relations, the indeterminates are given by all the elements of the set
A
and the
n^{th}
symmetric power is the set
\mathcal{M}_{n}(A)
of multisets of
n
elements of
A
ie. the set of "bags" of
n
elements of
A
, where a same element can possibly appear several times, ie. multisets, contrary to sets, take account of the multiplicity of its elements, but still not of their order. The differentiation is now given by a morphism of type
\oc_{n+1}A\rightarrow\oc_{n}A\otimes A
, for every
n\geq 0
. Given an homogenous polynomial
P\in R_{n+1}[x_{1},...,x_{p}]
, by differentiating, we obtain the sum
\underset{1\leq i\leq p}{\sum}\frac{\partial P}{\partial x_{i}}\otimes x_{i}
.

Given that it was the main example of
\mathbb{N}
-graded (co)differential category, and that we weren’t able to find many other interesting examples, we changed our focus to the question of finding conditions under which a
\mathbb{N}
-graded codifferential category verifies that
\oc_{n}
is necessarily the
n^{th}
symmetric power. In a
\mathbb{N}
-graded codifferential category, we also have multiplication maps
\oc_{n}A\otimes\oc_{p}A\rightarrow\oc_{n+p}A
and it appears that in the case where
\mathcal{C}
is not only enriched over commutative monoids but also over
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-modules, then if the differentiation
\oc_{n+1}A\rightarrow\oc_{n}A\otimes A
followed by the multiplication
\oc_{n}A\otimes A\rightarrow\oc_{n+1}
A is equal to
n.Id_{\oc_{n}A}
,
\oc_{n}A
is necessarily the
n^{th}
symmetric power of
A
. However, we do not have a clear proof for the moment. In fact, it seems that we don’t need the heavy categorical structure of
\mathbb{N}
-graded codifferential category with the many commutative diagrams of its definition in order to characterize the family of all symmetric powers of some objects in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category. All which matters seems to be the morphism
\oc_{n+1}A\rightarrow\oc_{n}A\otimes A
and
\oc_{n}A\otimes A\rightarrow\oc_{n+1}A
. In the case of symmetric powers, the structure of
\mathbb{N}
-graded codifferential category is closely related to the notion of
\mathbb{N}
-graded bialgebra. Classically a
\mathbb{N}
-graded bialgebra in the category of vector spaces is a bialgebra
A
which can be decomposed as a direct sum
A=\underset{n\geq 0}{\bigoplus}A_{n}
and such that the multiplication and the comultiplication respect in some way this decomposition. In
[
38
]
, we defined a
\mathbb{N}
-graded bialgebra, without this direct sum as a family
(A_{n})_{n\geq 0}
of objects equipped with a family of multiplications
\nabla_{n,p}:A_{n}\otimes A_{p}\rightarrow A_{n+p}
and a family of comultiplications
\Delta_{n,p}:A_{n+p}\rightarrow A_{n}\otimes A_{p}
, together with a unit map and a counit map which verify appropriate equations.

In the case of symmetric powers, the
0^{th}
symmetric power is just the monoidal unit of the category and thus the unit and counit maps are the identity and are not very interesting. That’s why we will not use units and counits in this paper. Also, the first symmetric power of an object
A
is just
A
. So, we will focus on the
n^{th}
symmetric power for
n\geq 2
. For us, a graded bimonoid (or bialgebra) in a symmetric monoidal category enriched over commutative monoids will be given by a family
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
of objects, together with multiplication maps
(\nabla_{n,p}:A_{n}\otimes A_{p}\rightarrow A_{n+p})_{n,p\geq 1}
and comultiplication maps
(\Delta_{n,p}:A_{n+p}\rightarrow A_{n}\otimes A_{p})_{n,p\geq 1}
such that only one axiom is required, which expresses
\nabla_{n,p};\Delta_{q,r}
, when
n+p=q+r
, in terms of the maps
\nabla_{a,b},\Delta_{c,d}
for
1\leq a,b,c,d\leq n-1
, combined in another way. And our main result is that if in addition to this axiom,
\Delta_{n,p};\nabla_{n,p}=\binom{n+p}{n}Id
, then
A_{n}
is necessarily the
n^{th}
symmetric power of
A_{1}
. We call binomial graded bimonoid such a family of objects, multiplications and comultiplications and the two axioms of a binomial graded bimonoid are expressed very elegantly with string diagrams, hence the name of this paper.

In a sequel to this paper, we plan to study binomial graded bimonoids in the general context of symmetric monoidal categories enriched over commutative monoids, ie. symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear categories, in which case several kinds of binomial graded bimonoids seem to exist, in particular, the one given by symmetric powers and the one given by divided powers, which are no longer the same.

Further references and related works

Note that several characterizations of the symmetric algebra in the classical setting of the category of vector spaces over a field of characteristic zero appeared in the literature
[
46
,
4
]
. However, in our opinion, none achieves the simplicity, and the constructive character, of our characterization of symmetric powers. One main reason must be that the axiom concerning the comultiplication followed by multiplication can be expressed easily only using our graded approach, without taking the biproducts of all the components of the algebra. It goes well with the general opinion that in linear logic or in the category of vector spaces, the multiplicative structure is more interesting than the additive one (eg.
[
18
]
or proof nets of linear logic
[
27
,
22
]
, or the axioms of a differential category). It seems that
[
4
]
expresses the same axiom in a non-graded setting, in a much more convoluted way than here. The notion of graded connected Hopf algebra is the object of several recent works
[
29
,
41
,
47
,
39
,
12
]
(A Hopf algebra
[
16
]
is a bialgebra with an antipode which is an additional linear map on top of the bialgebra structure, however, the antipode is not always included in the definition and in such case a Hopf algebra is the same as a bialgebra. Connected means that the graded object
(A_{n})_{n\geq 0}
verifies that
A_{0}\simeq I
which is implicit in our definition of binomial graded bimonoid: we don’t include this
A_{0}
in the definition because
I
is already part of the definition of a monoidal category and the unit, counit, multiplications
A_{0}\otimes A_{n}\rightarrow A_{n}
,
A_{n}\otimes A_{0}\rightarrow A_{n}
comultiplications
A_{n}\rightarrow A_{0}\otimes A_{n}
,
A_{n}\rightarrow A_{n}\otimes A_{0}
are already given by the unitors in the definitions of a symmetric monoidal category). Fock spaces have been discussed in the context of linear logic and categorical quantum mechanics, they are also used in quantum linear optics, on these subjects see
[
7
,
1
,
18
,
2
,
17
,
37
,
19
,
45
]
. In particular, path diagrams as presented in
[
19
]
were inspiring to us. General references on categories, monoidal categories and string diagrams are
[
40
,
36
,
44
]
. On random permutations, in connection with
Section

6
, see
[
20
,
30
,
31
,
6
]
. On graded algebras and coalgebras, see
[
3
]
. On matrices with prescribed row and column sums, in connection with
Proposition

21
, see the eponym article
[
5
]
. General references on algebra and notably tensor product of modules are
[
10
,
35
]
.

Overview

In
Section

2
, we define the main objects of the paper: permutation splittings and binomial graded bimonoids. Permutations splittings correspond to the usual definition of symmetric powers in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category, whereas binomial graded bimonoids are the algebraic structure that we will show characterize these symmetric powers in this same setting. We also define morphisms of permutation splittings, morphisms of binomial graded bimonoids and their reduced versions. It provides four categories defined for any symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category (the two categories of binomial graded bimonoids can more generally be defined in any symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category), and we define functors between them, that we will show are all isomorphisms of categories. Once defined, we state the main results of the paper that make these functors isomorphisms, under the form of a list of propositions which we show are consequences of the main body of the paper.

In
Section

3
, we explain how symmetric powers, divided powers, and permutation splittings are the same in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category.

In
Section

4
, we work on proving that every binomial graded bimonoid produces a permutation splitting, which is the most interesting direction in order to prove that this algebraic structure characterizes symmetric powers, in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category.

In
Section

5
, we prove that binomial graded bimonoids are associative and coassociative, which is not part of the two axioms of the definition but is a consequence of it. We also prove a corollary that will be useful later.

In
Section

6
, we introduce the notion of a blender, whose most basic properties we will use partly later. A blender is a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-convex combination of permutations, in other words, a random permutation. We introduce three different operations on them and list all the diagrams verified. Although we will not use all of them, we thought that these properties were sufficiently interesting to be included in the paper.

In
Section

7
, we go in the opposite direction of
Section

4
, ie. we prove that we obtain a binomial graded bimonoid from every permutation splitting.

In
Section

8
, we prove that this correspondence between permutation splittings and binomial graded bimonoids is bijective.

In
Section

9
, we look at morphisms of binomial graded bimonoids and morphisms of permutations splittings and their properties. Interestingly, only one of the two diagrams in the definition of binomial graded bimonoid is finally necessary because the two commutative diagrams of the definition that we gave in
Section

2
are in fact equivalent. Moreover, we show that morphisms of binomial graded bimonoids are always of the same simple form. The same story is true for permutation splittings.

In
Section

10
, we explain how in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category, a binomial graded bimonoid can be equipped with at most one structure of binomial graded bimonoid in the sense that two binomial graded bimonoids with the same underlying graded object are always isomorphic binomial graded bimonoids. In fact, we have a bit more: two binomial graded bimonoids such that the first object of the underlying graded object of the first one is isomorphic to the first object of the underlying graded object of the second one are then automatically isomorphic as binomial graded bimonoids. It shows that we were mistaken in
[
38
]
, when we first said that the family of symmetric powers of an object in the category of modules over a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-algebra can be equipped with two different structures of graded bialgebras. In fact, this structure is unique up to isomorphism even if it can show up in slightly different versions.

In
Section

11
, we give a few general results about base change in symmetric monoidal
k
-linear categories, ie. how we can change the semi-ring
k
without changing the underlying symmetric monoidal category. In particular, every symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category is a symmetric monoidal
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
-linear category, where
I
is the monoidal unit.

In
Section

12
, we look at examples of symmetric powers and binomial graded bimonoids, in the category
\mathbf{Rel}
and
\mathbf{Mod}_{R}
for
R
a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-algebra. We show how we can compute different, but isomorphic, binomial graded bimonoids starting from different permutation splittings in
\mathbf{Mod}_{R}
.

Notations and conventions

If
f:A\rightarrow B
and
g:B\rightarrow C
are two morphisms in the same category, the composite
A\rightarrow C
is written either
f;g
(diagrammatic order) or
g\circ f
(classical order). All the symmetric monoidal categories will be supposed to be strict monoidal. For
n\geq 0
, we will designate by
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
the symmetric group of order
n
. Note that we define
\mathfrak{S}_{0}:=\{\emptyset\}
, the group of permutations of
\emptyset
, with only element the empty function from
\emptyset
to
\emptyset
. In a symmetric monoidal category, the exchange allows one to define for every permutation
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
a natural transformation
\sigma:A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
that we will write using the same symbol. We will identify
\emptyset\in\mathfrak{S}_{0}
with
1_{I}:I\rightarrow I
. For every
n\geq 1
, we denote by
[1,n]
the set
\{1,...,n\}
of positive integers. If
M
is a multiset, its cardinal
|M|
is the sum of the multiplicities of all its elements. For every
n\geq 0
and set
X
, we note
\mathcal{M}_{n}(X)
the set of all multisets of elements of
X
which are of cardinal
n
. In the same way, we note
\mathcal{P}_{n}(X)
the set of all sets of
n
elements of
X
. If
M_{1}\in\mathcal{M}_{n_{1}}(X)
and
M_{2}\in\mathcal{M}_{n_{2}}(X)
, we denote
M_{1}\uplus M_{2}\in\mathcal{M}_{n_{1}+n_{2}}(X)
the sum of
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
which is the multiset whose multiplicity of every
x\in X
is the sum of the multiplicity of
x
in
M_{1}
and the multiplicity of
x
in
M_{2}
. A semi-ring is a set
R
which is a commutative monoid for the addition, a monoid for the multiplication, such that
0.r=0
and the multiplication distributes over the addition. A semi-ring morphism is a function between two semi-rings which is an additive and multiplicative morphism of monoids. The center
Z(R)
of a semi-ring is defined as the center of a ring and is a subsemi-ring of
R
which is commutative. An algebra over a commutative semi-ring
R
is a semi-ring
S
together with a morphism of semi-rings
S\rightarrow Z(R)
.
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
is the semi-ring of the nonnegative rational numbers. A (left) module over a semi-ring
R
is a set
M
which is an additive commutative monoid together with a map
R\times M\rightarrow M
which associates
r.m
to
(r,m)
, such that
1.m=m
,
0.m=r.0=0
,
(rr^{\prime}.m)=r.(r^{\prime}.m)
and this action distributes over each of the two additions. The definition of a right module over
R
is similar: the left action is replaced by a right action
M\times R\rightarrow M
such that in particular
m.(rr^{\prime})=(m.r).r^{\prime}
. If
R
,
S
are two semirings, a
(R,S)
-bimodule is a set
M
which is an additive commutative monoid together with a map
R\times M\rightarrow M
and a map
M\times S\rightarrow M
which make
M
a left
R
-module and a right
S
-module and such that
(r.m).s=r.(m.s)
. LHS means "left-hand side" and RHS means "right-hand side".

2
Categories of binomial graded bimonoids, permutation splittings, and functors between them

In this section, we define four categories starting from any symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category and explain how they are isomorphic as a consequence of the rest of the paper when the symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category is moreover enriched over
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-modules.

Definition 1
.

Let
k
be a commutative semi-ring. A symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category is a symmetric monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
such that every hom-set
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is a
k
-module and, moreover,
(f+g);h=(f;h)+(g;h)
,
f;(g+h)=(f;g)+(f;h)
,
0;f=f;0=0
,
(\lambda.f);g=\lambda.(f;g)=f;(\lambda.g)
,
(f+g)\otimes h=(f\otimes h)+(g\otimes h)
,
f\otimes(g+h)=(f\otimes g)+(f\otimes h)
,
0\otimes f=f\otimes 0=0
,
(\lambda.f)\otimes g=\lambda.(f\otimes g)=f\otimes(\lambda g)
.

Remark 2
.

Notice that a
\mathbb{N}
-module is exactly the same thing as a commutative monoid and that a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category is thus what is called an additive symmetric monoidal category in
[
9
,
8
,
38
]
ie. a symmetric monoidal category such that every hom-set is a commutative monoid all the axioms above which make no reference to the semi-ring
k
are verified.

Definition 3
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
be a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category. We define
PermSplit(\mathcal{C})
the category of permutation splittings of
\mathcal{C}
by:

•

Objects: families
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
together with two families of morphisms
(s_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\otimes n})_{n\geq 2}
and
(r_{n}:A_{1}^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A_{n})_{n\geq 2}
such that for every
n\geq 2:

•

Morphisms: a morphism from
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
to
(B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is given by a graded morphism
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
such that the following diagrams are commutative for every
n,p\geq 1
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}\otimes A_{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}\otimes B_{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n+p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n+p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n+p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n+p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}\otimes A_{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}\otimes B_{p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}\otimes f_{p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla_{n,p}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla_{n,p}^{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta_{n,p}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n+p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta_{n,p}^{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n+p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}\otimes f_{p}}

Remark 5
.

In the string diagrams, we write
n
instead of
A_{n}
.

Remark 6
.

Using the preceding convention about strings indexed by
0
, the axiom graded bimonoid is more generally true for every
(n,p,q,r)\in\mathbb{N}^{\times 4}
such that
n+p=q+r\geq 1
.

Definition 8
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
be a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category. We define
PermSplit_{1}(\mathcal{C})
the reduced category of permutation splittings of
\mathcal{C}
by:

•

Objects: families
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
together with two families of morphisms
(s_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\otimes n})_{n\geq 2}
and
(r_{n}:A_{1}^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A_{n})_{n\geq 2}
such that
s_{n};r_{n}=1_{A_{n}}
and
r_{n};s_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
for every
n\geq 2

•

Morphisms: a morphism from
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
to
(B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is given by a morphism
f_{1}:A_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}

Definition 9
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
be a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category. We define
BinGrBimon_{1}(\mathcal{C})
the reduced category of binomial graded bimonoids of
\mathcal{C}
by:

•

Objects: families
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
together with two families of morphisms
(s_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\otimes n})_{n\geq 2}
and
(r_{n}:A_{1}^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A_{n})_{n\geq 2}
such that
s_{n};r_{n}=1_{A_{n}}
and
r_{n};s_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
for every
n\geq 2

•

Morphisms: a morphism from
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
to
(B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is given by a morphism
f_{1}:A_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}

We will show in this paper that these four categories are isomorphic when
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category ie. we will define functors:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces BinGrBimon(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces PermSplit(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces PermSplit_{1}(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces BinGrBimon_{1}(\mathcal{C})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{3}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{3}}

such that:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{1}\circ G_{1}=Id_{PermSplit(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{1}\circ F_{1}=Id_{BinGrBinom(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{2}\circ G_{2}=Id_{PermSplit_{1}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{2}\circ F_{2}=Id_{PermSplit(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{3}\circ G_{3}=Id_{BinGrBinom_{1}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{3}\circ F_{3}=Id_{PermSplit_{1}(\mathcal{C})}}

From here and until the end of the paper, we suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category.

Let’s define these functors
F_{i},G_{i}
for
1\leq i\leq 3
. First on objects:

•

F_{1}\Big((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}:A_{n}\otimes A_{p}\rightarrow A_{n+p})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}:A_{n+p}\rightarrow A_{n}\otimes A_{p})_{n,p\geq 1}\Big)=\Big((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(s_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\otimes n})_{n\geq 2},(r_{n}:A_{1}^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A_{n})_{n\geq 2}\Big)
where
r_{n}
and
s_{n}
are defined by:

n\geq 1

We must verify that these functors actually define functions on objects and morphisms from the indicated domain to the indicated codomain ie. that they send objects from the domain category to objects of the codomain category and that they send morphisms of the domain category to morphisms of the codomain category. On objects, the non-trivial verifications amount to prove that the images by
F_{1}
are objects of
PermSplit(\mathcal{C})
and that the images by
G_{1}
are objects of
BinGrBimon(\mathcal{C})
. On morphisms, we must verify that the images by
F_{1}
are morphisms of
PermSplit(\mathcal{C})
, that the images by
G_{1}
are morphisms of
BinGrBimon(\mathcal{C})
, and that the images by
G_{2}
are morphisms of
PermSplit(\mathcal{C})
.

Most of the functorialities are trivial, except the one of
G_{2}
, more precisely the preservation of composition, the preservation of identities being a direct consequence of the equality
s_{n};r_{n}=Id
. Now, let’s look at the composites which must be equal to the identity. On objects, the most difficult to prove are
F_{1}\circ G_{1}=Id
and
G_{1}\circ F_{1}=Id
.
F_{2},G_{2}
being the identities on objects, it is immediate that they are inverse of each other. As to
F_{3},G_{3}
, because they are defined on objects as
G_{1},F_{1}
, they are inverse of each other iff
G_{1},F_{1}
are. On morphisms,
F_{1},G_{1}
and
F_{3},G_{3}
are the identities, so they are trivially inverses of each other. We only have to verify that
F_{2},G_{2}
are inverses of each other. It is immediate that
F_{2}\circ G_{2}=Id
.
G_{2}\circ F_{2}=Id
is more difficult. It amounts to the fact that a morphism of permutation splittings is always such that
f_{n}=s_{n};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}
for every
n\geq 2
.

We now sum up what we have to prove regarding the discussion above and show how each statement is a consequence of what is proved in the rest of the paper.

•

Images by
F_{1}
are objects of
PermSplit(\mathcal{C})
:

Proposition 10
.

If
((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p})_{n,p\geq 1})
is a graded binomial bimonoid, then we have:

:

Proposition 11
.

If
((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n})_{n\geq 1},(s_{n})_{n\geq 1})
is a permutation splitting, if we define
\nabla_{n,p}=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}
and
\Delta_{n,p}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}
, then we obtain a binomial graded bimonoid.

then
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings.

Proof.

Proposition

49
gives that
f_{n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}
and
Proposition

47
says that it is a sufficient condition for being a morphism of permutation splittings.

•

Images of morphisms by
G_{1}
are morphisms of
BinGrBinom(\mathcal{C})
:

Proposition 13
.

If
(f_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings, if we define

–

\nabla_{n,p}^{A}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};r_{n+p}^{A}

–

\nabla_{n,p}^{B}=s_{n}^{B}\otimes s_{p}^{B};r_{n+p}^{B}

–

\Delta_{n,p}^{A}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p}^{A};r_{n}^{A}\otimes r_{p}^{A}

–

\Delta_{n,p}^{B}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p}^{B};r_{n}^{B}\otimes r_{p}^{B}

where we put

–

s_{1}^{A}=r_{1}^{A}=Id_{A}

–

s_{1}^{B}=r_{1}^{B}=Id_{B}

then we have that
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of binomial graded bimonoids.

Proof.

Proposition

49
says that it is sufficient to prove that
f_{n}\otimes f_{p};\nabla_{n,p}^{B}=\nabla_{n,p}^{A};f_{n+p}
. We thus have to prove that

f_{n}\otimes f_{p};s_{n}^{B}\otimes s_{p}^{B};r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};r_{n+p}^{A};f_{n+p}

Moreover,
Proposition

47
gives that
f_{n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}
. We thus deduce
f_{n}\otimes f_{p};s_{n}^{B}\otimes s_{p}^{B};r_{n+p}^{B}=(s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B})\otimes(s_{p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes p};r_{p}^{B});s_{n}^{B}\otimes s_{p}^{B};r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n}^{B}\otimes r_{p}^{B};s_{n}^{B}\otimes s_{p}^{B};r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};(r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B})\otimes(r_{p}^{B};s_{p}^{B});r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};(\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}\sigma\otimes\tau);r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}^{B}

=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}\sigma;r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}^{B}

=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};r_{n+p}^{A};s_{n+p}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}^{B}=s_{n}^{A}\otimes s_{p}^{A};r_{n+p}^{A};f_{n+p}
. Note that we have used in particular the naturality of permutations, and the fact that
\sigma;r_{n}=r_{n}
for every
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
which is given by
Proposition

31
.
∎

•

Preservation of composition by
G_{2}
:

Proposition 14
.

If
f_{1}:A_{1}\rightarrow B_{1},g_{1}:B_{1}\rightarrow C_{1}
are morphisms, if
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
,
(B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
,
(C_{n})_{n\geq 1}
are permutation splittings, then we have
s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};g_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{C}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B};g_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{C}
.

Proof.

We compute
s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B};g_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{C}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;g_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{C}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};g_{1}^{\otimes n};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;r_{n}^{C}

=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};g_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{C}
.
∎

on objects:

.

((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n})_{n\geq 1},(s_{n})_{n\geq 1})

, and then

3
Symmetric powers in symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear categories

In this section, we show that symmetric powers can be defined in three equivalent ways in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category.

Definition 18
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
be a symmetric monoidal category and
A\in\mathcal{C}
. For every
n\geq 2
, the
n^{th}
symmetric power
S_{n}A
of
A
, if it exists, is defined as the coequalizer of this diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}

(1)

where there is one arrow for every
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
.

Proposition 19
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
be a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear symmetric monoidal category. Let
X\in\mathcal{C}
.For every
n\geq 2
, we define bijections between:

(a)

coequalizer
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}

of
Equation

1

(b)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

such that
u;v=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
and
v;u=1

(c)

equalizer
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

of
Equation

1

by associating:

(a\rightarrow b)

to
u
, the couple
(u,v)
where
v
is the unique arrow which makes this diagram commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

(b\rightarrow a)

to the couple
(u,v)
, the morphism
u

(b\rightarrow c)

to the couple
(u,v)
, the morphism
v

(c\rightarrow b)

to
v
, the couple
(u,v)
where
u
is the unique arrow which makes this diagram commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}

Proof.

We first verify that the images verify the required property.

(a\rightarrow b)

To start, note that
v
is correctly defined because for every
\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
,
\rho;\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\rho;\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\tau
by a change of variable. We already know that
u;v=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
.
v;u=1
is a consequence of the fact that
u
is an epimorphism as a colimit of
Equation

1
. Indeed, we have
u;v;u=(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma);u=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;u=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}u=\frac{1}{n!}(n!u)=u
, thus
u;(v;u)=u;1
and therefore
v;u=1
.

(b\rightarrow a)

We have
\sigma;u=\sigma;u;(v;u)=\sigma;(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\rho);u=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;\rho;u=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\gamma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\gamma;u
(the last step is by a change of variable). Therefore
u=\sigma^{-1};(\sigma;u)=\sigma^{-1};(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\gamma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\gamma;u)=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\gamma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma^{-1};\gamma;u=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\rho;u=\sigma;u
.

Suppose that
f:A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow Y
is such that the below diagram is commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

The below diagram is then commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v;f}

Indeed,
u;v;f=(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma);f=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;f=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}f=f
. Suppose now that
\phi:X\rightarrow Y
makes the below diagram commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

We then have
v;f=(v;u);\phi=1;\phi=\phi
.

(b\rightarrow c)

We have
v;\sigma=(v;u);v;\sigma=v;(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\rho);\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}v;\rho;\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\gamma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}v;\gamma
. Therefore
v=v;\sigma;\sigma^{-1}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\gamma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}v;\gamma;\sigma^{-1}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}v;\rho=v;\sigma
.

Suppose that
f:Y\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
is such that the below diagram is commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}

The below diagram is then commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f;u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

Indeed
f;u;v=f;(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma)=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}f;\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}f=f.
Suppose now that
\phi:Y\rightarrow X
makes the below diagram commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

We then have
f;u=\phi;(v;u)=\phi;1=\phi
.

(c\rightarrow b)

To start, note that
u
is correctly defined because for every
\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
,
(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma);\rho=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;\rho=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\tau
by a change of variable. We already know that
u;v=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
.
v;u=1
is a consequence of the fact that
v
is a monomorphism as a limit of
Equation

1
.
Indeed, we have
v;u;v=v;(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma)=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}v;\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma=v
, thus
v;u;v=v;1

and therefore
u;v=1
.

We now verify the bijectivities by checking that the appropriate composites are identities.

(a\rightarrow b\rightarrow a)

We associate a couple
(u,v)
to
u
and then
u
to
(u,v)
.

(b\rightarrow a\rightarrow b)

We associate
u
to
(u,v)
and then
(u,v)
to
u
because we know that
v
is the unique morphism
X\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
such that
u;v=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
.

(b\rightarrow c\rightarrow b)

We associate
v
to
(u,v)
and then
(u,v)
to
v
because we know that
u
is the unique morphism
A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow X
such that
u;v=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
.

(c\rightarrow b\rightarrow c)

We associate a couple
(u,v)
to
v
and then
v
to
(u,v)
.

∎

\Delta_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{q}}\colon A_{n_{1}+\cdots+n_{q}}\rightarrow A_{n_{1}}\otimes\ldots\otimes A_{n_{q}}
from
q=2
to every
q\geq 2
(where
n_{1},...,n_{q}\geq 0
and by defining
\Delta_{n,0}=\Delta_{0,n}=1_{A_{n}}
) by induction:

\Delta_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{q+1}}=\Delta_{n_{1}+\cdots+n_{q},n_{q+1}};\Delta_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{q}}\otimes A_{n_{q+1}}

where the sum is indexed over the matrices
(i_{\alpha}^{\beta})_{(\alpha,\beta)\in[1,q]\times[1,r]}
with coefficients in
\mathbb{N}
such that for
every
\beta\in[1,r]
,
\underset{1\leq\alpha\leq q}{\sum}i_{\alpha}^{\beta}=p_{\beta}
and for every
\alpha\in[1,q]
,

\underset{1\leq\beta\leq r}{\sum}i_{\alpha}^{\beta}=n_{\alpha}
.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on
(q,r)
. The case
(2,2)
is the axiom of a graded bimonoid. Suppose that the cases
(k,l)
are true for every
2\leq k\leq q
and
2\leq l\leq r
where
q,r
are two integers
\geq 2
. Let’s prove that the cases
(q+1,l)
where
2\leq l\leq r
are true which will give us that all the cases
(k,l)
where
2\leq k\leq q+1
and
2\leq l\leq r
are true. We have:

In the second step, we used the induction hypothesis for
(2,l)
and in the third step for
(q,l)
. We now justify the last step. Clearly, every term of the LHS is a term of the RHS. Reciprocally, consider a term of the RHS. Put
J_{1}=u_{q+1}^{1},\ldots,J_{l}=u_{q+1}^{l}
and
I_{1}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{q}^{1},\ldots,I_{l}=u_{1}^{l}+\cdots+u_{q}^{l}
. We then have
I_{1}+J_{1}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{q}^{1}+u_{q+1}^{1}=p_{1},\ldots,I_{l}+J_{l}=u_{1}^{l}+\cdots+u_{q}^{l}+u_{q+1}^{l}=p_{l},I_{1}+\cdots+I_{l}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{q}^{1}+\cdots.+u_{1}^{l}+\cdots+u_{q}^{l}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{1}^{l}+\cdots+u_{q}^{1}+\cdots+u_{q}^{l}=n_{1}+\cdots+n_{q}
and
J_{1}+\cdots+J_{l}=u_{q+1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{q+1}^{l}=n_{q+1}
. It is thus a term of the LHS. Finally, the LHS and the RHS contain the same terms and are thus equal.

Let’s now prove that the cases
(k,r+1)
where
2\leq k\leq q
are true which will give us that all the cases
(k,l)
where
2\leq k\leq q
and
2\leq l\leq r+1
are true. We have:

In the second step, we used the induction hypothesis for
(k,2)
and in the third step for
(k,r)
.
We now justify the last step. Clearly, every term of the LHS is a term of the RHS. Reciprocally, consider a term of the RHS. Put
J_{1}=u_{1}^{r+1},\ldots,J_{k}=u_{k}^{r+1}
and
I_{1}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{1}^{r},\dots,I_{k}=u_{k}^{1}+\cdots+u_{k}^{r}
. We then have
I_{1}+J_{1}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{1}^{r}+u_{1}^{r+1}=n_{1},\ldots,I_{k}+J_{k}=u_{k}^{1}+\cdots+u_{k}^{r}+u_{k}^{r+1}=n_{k},I_{1}+\cdots+I_{k}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{1}^{r}+\cdots+u_{k}^{1}+\cdots+u_{k}^{r}=u_{1}^{1}+\cdots+u_{k}^{1}+\cdots+u_{1}^{r}+\cdots+u_{k}^{r}=p_{1}+\cdots+p_{r}
and
J_{1}+\cdots+J_{k}=u_{1}^{r+1}+\cdots+u_{k}^{r+1}=p_{r+1}
. It is thus a term of the LHS. Finally, the LHS and the RHS contain the same terms and are thus equal.
∎

.

The matrices
(i_{\alpha}^{\beta})_{1\leq\alpha,\beta\leq q}
contain only
0
and
1
coefficients and are such that there is exactly one
1
in every column and exactly one
1
in every line. This is called a permutation matrix. In string diagrams, it amounts to the fact that in every summand of the RHS, every input is related to exactly one output by a line containing a
1
and not a
0
and no two different inputs are related in this way to the same output. We can then cut the lines containing a
0
and we end up with every summand of the RHS being one of the permutations of
\mathfrak{S}_{q}
, moreover, each of these permutations appears exactly once in the sum.
∎

Proof.

By induction on
q
. For
q=2
, it is given by the second axiom of a binomial graded bimonoid. Suppose that it is true for some
q\geq 2
. We then have
\Delta_{1,\ldots,1};\nabla_{1,\ldots,1}
(
q+1
times 1)
=\Delta_{q,1};\Delta_{1,\ldots,1}\otimes 1;\nabla_{1,\ldots,1}\otimes 1;\nabla_{q,1}
(
q
times
1
) =
q!\Delta_{q,1};\nabla_{q,1}=q!\binom{q+1}{1}.Id=q!(q+1).Id=(q+1)!.Id
.
∎

Corollary 24
.

If
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category and
(A_{n}\in\mathcal{C})_{n\geq 1}
can be equipped with a structure of binomial graded bimonoid, then for every
n\geq 2
,
A_{n}
is the
n^{th}
symmetric power of
A_{1}
.

Proof.

Define
r_{n}:=\nabla_{1,...,1}
and
s_{n}:=\frac{1}{n!}\Delta_{1,...,1}
. It then follows from
Corollary

22
,
Proposition

23
and
Proposition

19
.
∎

5
Associativity of binomial graded bimonoids

In preparation for the proof of the bijectivity of
F_{1}
, we infer some restricted versions of (higher-order) associativity and coassociativity directly from the axioms of binomial graded bimonoid.

Proof.

If
n,p
or
q
is equal to
0
, it is easily shown to be true. We then make the proof for
n,p,q\geq 1
by induction on
n+p+q
. We will use the fact that
\Delta_{n,1}
is a monomorphism thanks to the equation
\Delta_{n,1};\nabla_{n,1}=(n+1).Id
. We thus prove that
\nabla_{n,p}\otimes A_{q};\nabla_{n+p,q};\Delta_{n+p+q-1,1}=A_{n}\otimes\nabla_{p,q};\nabla_{n,p+q};\Delta_{n+p+q-1,1}
and deduce associativity by the fact that
\Delta_{n+p+q-1,1}
is a monomorphism. It follows that we prove a bit more than what is announced in the proposition: every graded bimonoid in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category such that
\Delta_{n,p}
is a monomorphism is associative (and it is coassociative if
\nabla_{n,p}
is an epimorphism). We borrow this idea of monomorphism from
[
3
]
where a graded algebra with such epimorphic multiplications and a graded coalgebra with such monomorphic multiplications are called strongly graded.

Case
(1,1,1)
ie.
n+p+q=3
:

(2)

In the first step, we used the compatiblity multiplication/comultiplication. In the second step, we used it a second time. In the third step, we only rewrote the string diagrams differently. In the fourth step, we used the induction hypothesis (on the left) and the case where two entries are equal to
0
(on the right). In the last step, we changed the names of the indexes.

We now verify that the terms in
Equation

1
and
Equation

2
are exactly the same. If we choose a term in
Equation

1
we can verify that it is also a term of
Equation

2
by putting:
a^{\prime}:=e,b^{\prime}:=f,c^{\prime}:=g+c,d^{\prime}:=d+h,e^{\prime}:=g,f^{\prime}:=h,g^{\prime}:=c,h^{\prime}:=d
. If we chose a term in
Equation

2
, we can verify that it is then also a term of
Equation

1
by putting:
a:=a^{\prime}+e^{\prime},b:=b^{\prime}+f^{\prime},c:=g^{\prime},d:=h^{\prime},e:=a^{\prime},f:=b^{\prime},g:=e^{\prime},h:=f^{\prime}
. The proposition is thus true for
n+p+q=k+1
.
∎

Remark 26
.

The dual of
Proposition

25
is also true, ie. binomial graded bimonoids are coassociative. As well, we will not phrase explicitly the duals of the two following corollaries. However, we will use them later.

.

where we used the induction hypothesis on the entries
n_{1}+n_{2},n_{3},...,n_{p+1}
and then the base case on the entries
n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}+...+n_{p+1}
. So it is true for
p+1
.

∎

6
Blenders

Blenders are
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-convex combinations of permutations of the same order in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category. In this section, we define blenders and look at their properties. We will use some of these properties later.

Definition 29
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category. A
n
-blender is a natural transformation of the form
\frac{1}{|M|}\underset{\sigma\in M}{\sum}\sigma:A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
for some
n\geq 0
and nonempty multiset
M\in\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{S}_{n})
.

We will write
\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
for the set of
n
-blenders of a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category
\mathcal{C}
which are of the form
\frac{1}{|M|}\underset{\sigma\in M}{\sum}\sigma
for some nonempty multiset
M\in\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{S}_{n})
of cardinal
m
. The set of all
n
-blenders of
\mathcal{C}
is then given by
\mathbf{S}_{n}(\mathcal{C})=\underset{m\geq 1}{\bigsqcup}\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
. We then have

\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cong\mathbf{S}_{n}^{1}(\mathcal{C})
as groups. An element of
\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
is called
a
(n,m)
-blender. Permutations are thus the

(n,1)
-blenders and for every
n\geq 0,\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S_{n}}}{\sum}\sigma
is a
(n,n!)
-blender.

Proposition 30
.

Permutations are blenders and blenders are stable by tensor product and composition. More precisely: permutations
A^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n}
are
n
-blenders, the tensor product of a
n
-blender with a
p
-blender is a
(n+p)
-blender and the composition of two
n
-blenders is a
n
-blender.

Proof.

Permutations are blenders associated with a singleton multiset.

Stability by tensor product:
\Big(\frac{1}{|M_{1}|}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}}{\sum}\sigma\Big)\otimes\Big(\frac{1}{|M_{2}|}\underset{\rho\in M_{2}}{\sum}\rho\Big)=\frac{1}{|M_{1}||M_{2}|}\underset{\nu\in M_{1}\otimes M_{2}}{\sum}\nu=\frac{1}{|M_{1}\otimes M_{2}|}\underset{\nu\in M_{1}\otimes M_{2}}{\sum}\nu
(where
M_{1}\otimes M_{2}=[\sigma\otimes\rho,\sigma\in M_{1},\rho\in M_{2}]
).

Stability by composition:
\Big(\frac{1}{|M_{1}|}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}}{\sum}\sigma\Big);\Big(\frac{1}{|M_{2}|}\underset{\rho\in M_{2}}{\sum}\rho\Big)=\frac{1}{|M_{1}||M_{2}|}\underset{\nu\in M_{1};M_{2}}{\sum}\nu=\frac{1}{|M_{1};M_{2}|}\underset{\nu\in M_{1};M_{2}}{\sum}\nu
(where

M_{;}M_{2}=[\sigma;\rho,\sigma\in M_{1},\rho\in M_{2}]
).
∎

Proposition 31
.

s_{n}
is invariant by postcomposition by
n
-blenders and
r_{n}
is invariant by precomposition by
n
-blenders.

Proof.

We already know that
s_{n}
is invariant by postcomposition by permutations ie. if
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
, then
s_{n};\sigma=s_{n}
. We thus have
s_{n};\Big(\frac{1}{|M|}\underset{\sigma\in M}{\sum}\sigma\Big)=\frac{1}{|M|}\underset{\sigma\in M}{\sum}s_{n};\sigma=\frac{1}{|M|}\underset{\sigma\in M}{\sum}s_{n}=\frac{1}{|M|}|M|s_{n}=s_{n}
. Same for
r_{n}
.
∎

The following proposition defines and states some properties of three operations on blenders: sum, tensor product and composition. We will only use the composition and tensor product of blenders later on but we included the sum
\boxplus
for completeness because it verifies interesting algebraic properties. Note that the grading is very important here and introduces a strong "typed" flavour which ensures that the operations are correctly defined. One can only compose and sum blenders with permutations of the same order and it is crucial to know the number of permutations in two blenders when we sum them.

Proposition 32
.

(\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m}(\mathcal{C}))_{n\geq 0,m\geq 1}
is a (noncommutative, without additive unit) "graded semi-ring" in two different ways, in the sense that we have an addition:

\boxplus_{n}^{m_{1},m_{2}}\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})&\rightarrow\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})\\
(x,y)&\mapsto x\boxplus y:=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}(m_{1}x+m_{2}y)\end{aligned}\right.

and two multiplications:

\otimes_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{m_{1},m_{2}}\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})&\rightarrow\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}+n_{2}}^{m_{1}.m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})\\
(x,y)&\mapsto x\otimes y\end{aligned}\right.

;_{n}^{m_{1},m_{2}}\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})&\rightarrow\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{1}.m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})\\
(x,y)&\mapsto x;y\end{aligned}\right.

with respective multiplicative units:

\begin{aligned} 1_{I}\in\mathbf{S}_{0}^{1}(\mathcal{C}),\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} 1_{\_^{\otimes n}}\in\mathbf{S}_{n}^{1}(\mathcal{C})\end{aligned}

such that:

x\boxplus y=y\boxplus x

(x\boxplus y)\boxplus z=x\boxplus(y\boxplus z)

(x\otimes y)\otimes z=x\otimes(y\otimes z)

(x;y);z=x;(y;z)

1_{I}\otimes x=x\otimes 1_{I}=x

1_{\_^{\otimes n}};x=x;1_{\_^{\otimes n}}=x

(x\boxplus y)\otimes z=(x\otimes z)\boxplus(y\otimes z)

x\otimes(y\boxplus z)=(x\otimes y)\boxplus(x\otimes z)

(x\boxplus y);z=(x;z)\boxplus(y;z)

x;(y\boxplus z)=(x;y)\boxplus(x;z)

Note that there is no additive unit for
\boxplus
. If we want to make clear using the gradings to which elements these equalities apply, and that they are correctly defined, we can state them by saying that the below diagrams are commutative:

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{11.2557pt}{-26.77249pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\qquad(\mbox{right unitality of }1_{\_^{\otimes n}}\mbox{ with respect to };)

Proof.

Let
n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}\geq 0
and
M_{1}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{S}_{n_{1}}),M_{2}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{S}_{n_{2}}),M_{3}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{S}_{n_{3}})
. Write
m_{1}:=|M_{1}|,m_{2}:=|M_{2}|
and
m_{3}:=|M_{3}|
and consider
x\in\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{C}),y\in\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{C}),z\in\mathbf{S}_{n_{3}}^{m_{3}}(\mathcal{C})
such that:

x_{A}=\frac{1}{m_{1}}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}}{\sum}\sigma:A^{\otimes n_{1}}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n_{1}}

y_{A}=\frac{1}{m_{2}}\underset{\sigma\in M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma:A^{\otimes n_{2}}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n_{2}}

z_{A}=\frac{1}{m_{3}}\underset{\sigma\in M_{3}}{\sum}\sigma:A^{\otimes n_{3}}\rightarrow A^{\otimes n_{3}}

We verify that if
n_{1}=n_{2}=n
, then
x\boxplus y\in\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})
, that
x\otimes y\in\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}+n_{2}}^{m_{1}.m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})
and that if
n_{1}=n_{2}=n
, then
x;y\in\mathbf{S}_{n}^{m_{1}.m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})
:

\displaystyle x\boxplus y

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\bigg(m_{1}\frac{1}{m_{1}}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}}{\sum}\sigma+m_{2}\frac{1}{m_{2}}\underset{\sigma\in M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}\uplus M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|M_{1}\uplus M_{2}|}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}\uplus M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma

\displaystyle x\otimes y

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}}\underset{\sigma_{1}\in M_{1}}{\sum}\sigma_{1}\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{2}}\underset{\sigma_{2}\in M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma_{2}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}m_{2}}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma_{1}\in M_{1}\\
\sigma_{2}\in M_{2}\end{subarray}}{\sum}\sigma_{1}\otimes\sigma_{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|M_{1}\otimes M_{2}|}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1}\otimes M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma

\displaystyle x;y

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}}\underset{\sigma_{1}\in M_{1}}{\sum}\sigma_{1}\bigg);\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{2}}\underset{\sigma_{2}\in M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma_{2}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}m_{2}}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma_{1}\in M_{1}\\
\sigma_{2}\in M_{2}\end{subarray}}{\sum}\sigma_{1};\sigma_{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|M_{1};M_{2}|}\underset{\sigma\in M_{1};M_{2}}{\sum}\sigma

We now verify the least obvious algebraic properties (those concerning
\boxplus
, except the commutativity).

\displaystyle(x\boxplus y)\boxplus z

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}\big((m_{1}+m_{2})\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}(m_{1}x+m_{2}y)+m_{3}z\big)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{1}x+m_{2}y+m_{3}z)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{1}x+(m_{2}+m_{3})\frac{1}{m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{2}y+m_{3}z))

\displaystyle=x\boxplus(y\boxplus z)

\displaystyle(x\boxplus y)\otimes z

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}(m_{1}x+m_{2}y)\bigg)\otimes z

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}(m_{1}.x\otimes z+m_{2}.y\otimes z)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}m_{3}+m_{2}m_{3}}(m_{1}m_{3}.x\otimes z+m_{2}m_{3}.y\otimes z)

\displaystyle=(x\otimes z)\boxplus(y\otimes z)

\displaystyle x\otimes(y\boxplus z)

\displaystyle=x\otimes\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{2}y+m_{3}z)\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{2}.x\otimes y+m_{3}.x\otimes z)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{1}m_{2}+m_{1}m_{3}}(m_{1}m_{2}.x\otimes y+m_{1}m_{3}.x\otimes z)

\displaystyle=(x\otimes y)\boxplus(x\otimes z)

\displaystyle(x\boxplus y);z

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}(m_{1}x+m_{2}y)\bigg);z

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}(m_{1}(x;z)+m_{2}(y;z))\bigg)

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}m_{3}+m_{2}m_{3}}(m_{1}m_{3}(x;z)+m_{2}m_{3}(y;z))\bigg)

\displaystyle=(x;z)\boxplus(y;z)

\displaystyle x;(y\boxplus z)

\displaystyle=x;\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{2}y+m_{3}z)\bigg)

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{2}+m_{3}}(m_{2}(x;y)+m_{3}(x;z))\bigg)

\displaystyle=\bigg(\frac{1}{m_{1}m_{2}+m_{1}m_{3}}(m_{1}m_{2}(x;y)+m_{1}m_{3}(x;z))\bigg)

\displaystyle=(x;y)\boxplus(x;z)

The other equations are very easy to verify.
∎

Remark 33
.

The functoriality of
\otimes
also implies that

\displaystyle(x\otimes y);(z\otimes w)=(x;z)\otimes(y;w)

whenever it makes sense ie. that this diagram is commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{3}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{4}}(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{3}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{4}}(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}+n_{2}}^{m_{1}.m_{3}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}+n_{2}}^{m_{2}.m_{4}}(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}}^{m_{1}.m_{2}}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathbf{S}_{n_{2}}^{m_{3}.m_{4}}(\mathcal{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{S}_{n_{1}+n_{2}}^{m_{1}.m_{2}.m_{3}.m_{4}}(\mathcal{C})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\otimes\gamma\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces;_{n_{1}}^{m_{1},m_{2}}\times;_{n_{2}}^{m_{3},m_{4}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{m_{1},m_{3}}\times\otimes_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{m_{2},m_{4}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces;_{n_{1}.n_{2}}^{m_{1}.m_{3},m_{2}.m_{4}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{m_{1}.m_{2},m_{3}.m_{4}}}

7
From permutation splittings to binomial graded bimonoids

In this section, we verify that
G_{1}
is well-defined on objects ie. that from a permutation splitting, it produces a binomial graded bimonoid. In order to prove that we obtain a binomial graded bimonoid, we first prove seemingly stronger properties. In this section we write
\nabla_{n,p}^{*}
and
\Delta_{n,p}^{*}
and add stars in the same way in the string diagrams to denote the multiplications and comultiplications which are defined by
G_{1}
starting from
s_{n},r_{n}
ie.
\nabla_{n,p}^{*}:=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}
and
\Delta_{n,p}^{*}:=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}
. Remember that in this context, we define
r_{1}=s_{1}=1_{A_{1}}
.

Proof.

We prove it using in-line notations:

\displaystyle\nabla_{n,p}\otimes 1_{q};\nabla_{n+p,q}

\displaystyle=s_{n}\otimes s_{p}\otimes 1_{q};r_{n+p}\otimes 1_{q};s_{n+p}\otimes s_{q};r_{n+p+q}

\displaystyle=s_{n}\otimes s_{p}\otimes s_{q};\left(\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}\sigma\right)\otimes 1_{q};r_{n+p+q}

\displaystyle=s_{n}\otimes s_{p}\otimes s_{q};r_{n+p+q}

but we also have:

\displaystyle 1_{n}\otimes\nabla_{p,q};\nabla_{n,p+q}

\displaystyle=1_{n}\otimes s_{p}\otimes s_{q};1_{n}\otimes r_{p+q};s_{n}\otimes s_{p+q};r_{n+p+q}

\displaystyle=s_{n}\otimes s_{p}\otimes s_{q};1_{n}\otimes\left(\frac{1}{(p+q)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{p+q}}{\sum}\sigma\right);r_{n+p+q}

\displaystyle=s_{n}\otimes s_{p}\otimes s_{q};r_{n+p+q}

hence the equality.
∎

Proof.

\Delta_{n,p}^{*};\nabla_{n,p}^{*}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma)\otimes(\frac{1}{p!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}}{\sum}\rho);r_{n+p}

=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}\sigma\otimes\rho;r_{n+p}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};r_{n+p}=\binom{n+p}{n}1_{n+p}

∎

Remark 40
.

In accordance with the definition of binomial graded bimonoid, in the RHS of the above equation, if
a,b,c
or
d
is equal to
0
, the string diagram must be interpreted as the one obtained by erasing the string indexed by
0
.

Proof.

We use that the part in red below is equal to
(q-k)
times a
q
-blender which is preceded by
s_{q}
and can thus be erased, and also that
\frac{q-k}{k+1}\binom{q}{k}=\frac{q!(q-k)}{(q-k)!k!(k+1)}=\frac{q!}{(q-k-1)!(k+1)!}=\binom{q}{k+1}
(in the diagram below, the index
k
denotes the
k^{th}
string from the left and not
A_{k}
. Indexes
1,N...
are thus now used to distinguish between several occurrences of
A_{1}
):

\sigma^{\prime}=\sigma;(J,N+1)
and
\sigma^{\prime\prime}=\sigma^{\prime}_{|[1,N]}
(given that
\sigma^{\prime}(N+1)=N+1
,
\sigma^{\prime\prime}
denotes the permutation of order
N
such that
\sigma^{\prime}=\sigma^{\prime\prime}\otimes 1_{A_{1}}
. Then
\sigma^{\prime};r_{N}\otimes r_{1}=\sigma^{\prime\prime}\otimes 1_{A_{1}};r_{N}\otimes r_{1}=(\sigma^{\prime\prime};r_{N})\otimes(1_{A_{1}};r_{1})=r_{N}\otimes r_{1}
. We can then write:

Lemma 43

s_{p}
equalizes all the permutations in
\mathfrak{S}_{p}
. To obtain the third diagram, we use that we have summed
p
times the same term. This diagram is equal to the second term in the RHS of the statement of the lemma, by definition of
\Delta_{p-1,1}^{*}
and
\nabla_{n,p-1}^{*}
.

To obtain the first diagram, we use
Lemma

42
which gives that if
\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{S}_{N+1}
, and
\sigma^{-1}(N+1)=(\sigma^{\prime})^{-1}(N+1)
, then
\sigma;r_{N}\otimes r_{1}=\sigma^{\prime};r_{N}\otimes r_{1}
. The second diagram is obtained by adding the blender depicted in red. The third diagram is obtained by using that
s_{n}
is an equalizer (ie. we can perform any permutation just after
s_{n}
without changing the value of the string diagram). To obtain the fourth diagram, we use that we have summed
n
times the same term. This diagram is equal to the first term in the RHS of the statement of the lemma, by definition of
\Delta_{n-1,1}^{*}
and
\nabla_{n-1,p}^{*}
.
∎

Lemma 44
.

For all
n\geq 1,p\geq 0
,
k\geq 0
,
a\geq 1
and
b,c,d\geq 0
such that
a+b=n
,
c+d=p
,
b+d=k
and
a+c=n+p-k

In the first step, we used associativity, in the second step coassociativity, in the third step commutativity (
Proposition

36
), in the fourth step associativity and in the fifth step the compatibility comultiplication/multiplication.
∎

We can now use these lemmas to prove our proposition.

Proof of
Proposition

39
.

We’re going to prove that for every

If
n=0
(and thus
p\geq 1
): the two sides of the equation are equal to
\Delta_{p-1,1}^{*}
.

If
p=0
(and thus
n\geq 1
): the two sides of the equation are equal to
\Delta_{n-1,1}^{*}
.

•

We now fix
n,p\geq 0
such that
n+p\geq 1
and prove the equality for every
1\leq k\leq n+p-1
by induction on
k
. Suppose it is true for some
1\leq k\leq n+p-1
such that
k+1\leq n+p-1
. We show that it is true for
k+1
. We use
Lemma

41
, then the induction hypothesis, then the case
k=1
(we know that for every term in the sum,
a+c=n+p-k\geq 1
, thus
a+c\geq 1
, and we separate accordingly the sum into the cases such that
a\geq 1
and the ones such that
c\geq 1
), then
Lemma

44
. In the fifth step, we use a change of variable in each of the two sums. In the sixth step, we use that the general term of the first sum is equal to
0
when
v=0
, thus we can include indexes such that
v=0
in the sum, without changing its value. Same thing with
x
in the second sum. In the last step, we use that
v+x=k+1
and simplify the fraction.

8
Bijectivity of the correspondence

In this section, we verify that
F_{1}
and
G_{1}
are inverse of each other on objects ie. that if we start with a permutation splitting, apply
G_{1}
and then
F_{1}
, we recover the same permutation splitting and conversely if we start with a binomial graded bimonoid, apply
F_{1}
and then
G_{1}
, we recover the same binomial graded bimonoid.

Proposition 45
.

F_{1};G_{1}=Id
on objects.

Notice that
\frac{1}{(n+p!)}\binom{n+p}{n}=\frac{1}{n!p!}
. The equality then follows by the dual of what’s preceding.
∎

}}

We proceed with in-line equations. We must show that
r_{n}^{*}=r_{n}
ie. that
s_{1}^{\otimes n};((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1);s_{n}
. First note that
s_{1}=1
and thus that
r_{n}^{*}=((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1);r_{n}
. Then notice that
((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1)
is a blender which is annihilated by the following
r_{n}
, thus
r_{n}^{*}=r_{n}
.
We must also show that
s_{n}^{*}=s_{n}
ie. that
\frac{1}{n!}\binom{n}{n-1}\binom{n-1}{n-2}...\binom{2}{1}s_{n};((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1);((r_{n-2};s_{n-2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1);r_{1}^{\otimes n}=s_{n}
. First notice that
\binom{n}{n-1}\binom{n-1}{n-2}...\binom{2}{1}=n(n-1)...2=n!
and thus that
s_{n}^{*}=s_{n};((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1);((r_{n-2};s_{n-2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1);r_{1}^{\otimes n}
. Then notice that
r_{1}=1
and thus that
s_{n}^{*}=s_{n};((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1);((r_{n-2};s_{n-2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1)
. Finally we use that
((r_{n-1};s_{n-1})\otimes 1);((r_{n-2};s_{n-2})\otimes 1);...;((r_{2};s_{2})\otimes 1)
is a blender and thus
s_{n}^{*}=s_{n}
.
∎

9
Morphisms of binomial graded bimonoids and morphisms of permutation splittings

In this section, we show that morphisms of binomial graded bimonoids in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category can be characterized in three equivalent ways, which are simpler than the definition we gave. The same is true for morphisms of splitting idempotents. We start with morphisms of splitting idempotents.

Proposition 47
.

Let
((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n}^{A})_{n\geq 2},(s_{n}^{A})_{n\geq 2})
,
((B_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n}^{B})_{n\geq 2},(s_{n}^{B})_{n\geq 2})
be two permutation splittings in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category and
(f_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
be a graded morphism. Then
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings iff any of the three following conditions is verified for every
n\geq 2
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{n}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{n}^{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}^{\otimes n}}

(2)

f_{n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}

(3)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}^{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}}

(4)

Thus, the definition of morphism of permutation splittings that we gave is redundant. In fact, we have a bit more:

Lemma 48
.

Let
n\geq 2
,
A_{1},A_{n},B_{1},B_{n}
objects in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category and
r_{n}^{A}:A_{1}^{\otimes n}\rightarrow A_{n}
,
s_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\otimes n}
two morphisms such that
r_{n}^{A};s_{n}^{A}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
,
r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
and
s_{n}^{A};r_{n}^{A}=Id_{A_{n}}
,
s_{n}^{B};r_{n}^{B}=Id_{B_{n}}
. The three following conditions are then equivalent:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{n}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{n}^{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}^{\otimes n}}

(5)

f_{n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}

(6)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}^{\otimes n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}^{\otimes n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}^{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}}

(7)

Proof.

Suppose
Equation

5
is verified. We then have:

s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=f_{n};s_{n}^{B};r_{n}^{B}=f_{n};Id_{B_{n}}=f_{n}

Thus
Equation

6
is verified. Suppose now that
Equation

6
is verified. We then have:

r_{n}^{A};f_{n}=r_{n}^{A};s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}f_{1}^{\otimes n};\sigma;r_{n}^{B}

But we also have for every
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
:

\sigma;r_{n}^{B}=\sigma;r_{n}^{B};Id_{B_{n}}=\sigma;r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B};r_{n}^{B}=\sigma;\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\tau;r_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;\tau;r_{n}^{B}

=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\rho;r_{n}^{B}=r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B};r_{n}^{B}=r_{n}^{B};Id_{B_{n}}=r_{n}^{B}

And thus

r_{n}^{A};f_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}(n!)f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}

ie.
Equation

7
is verified. Suppose now that
Equation

7
is verified. We then have:

s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=s_{n}^{A};r_{n}^{A};f_{n}=Id_{A_{n}};f_{n}=f_{n}

Thus
Equation

6
is verified. Suppose now that
Equation

6
is verified. We then have:

f_{n};s_{n}^{B}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};\sigma=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}s_{n}^{A};\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes n}

But we also have for every
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
:

s_{n}^{A};\sigma=Id_{A_{n}};s_{n}^{A};\sigma=s_{n}^{A};r_{n}^{A};s_{n}^{A};\sigma=s_{n}^{A};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\tau;\sigma=s_{n}^{A};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\rho

=s_{n}^{A};r_{n}^{A};s_{n}^{A}=Id_{A_{n}};s_{n}^{A}=s_{n}^{A}

And then:

f_{n};s_{n}^{B}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n}=\frac{1}{n!}(n!)s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n}

Thus
Equation

5
is verified.
∎

Proposition

47
follows. We now continue with morphisms of binomial graded bimonoids.

Proposition 49
.

Let
((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}^{A})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}^{A})_{n,p\geq 1})
,
((B_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}^{A})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}^{A})_{n,p\geq 1})
be two binomial graded bimonoids in a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category and
(f_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
be a graded morphism. Then
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of binomial graded bimonoids iff
Equation

8
is verified for every
n,p\geq 1
,
Equation

9
is verified for every
n\geq 2
or
Equation

10
is verified for every
n,p\geq 1
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}\otimes A_{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}\otimes B_{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n+p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n+p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}\otimes f_{p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla_{n,p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla_{n,p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n+p}}

(8)

f_{n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}

(9)

where we define:

(13)

Proof.

Suppose that
Equation

11
is verified. We then have
f_{1}^{\otimes k};r_{k}=r_{k};f_{k}
for every
2\leq k\leq n
, by induction:
f_{1}^{\otimes 2};r_{2}=f_{1}^{\otimes 2};\nabla_{1,1}=\nabla_{1,1};f_{2}=r_{2};f_{2}
. Now suppose that it is true for some
2\leq k\leq n-1
, we then have
f_{1}^{\otimes(k+1)};r_{k+1}=f_{1}^{\otimes k}\otimes f_{1};r_{k}\otimes Id_{A_{1}};\nabla_{k,1}=(f_{1}^{\otimes k};r_{k})\otimes f_{1};\nabla_{k,1}=(r_{k};f_{k})\otimes f_{1};\nabla_{k,1}=(r_{k}\otimes Id_{A_{1}});(f_{k}\otimes f_{1});\nabla_{k,1}=(r_{k}\otimes Id_{A_{1}});\nabla_{k,1};f_{k+1}=r_{k+1};f_{k+1}
. We thus have
s_{k};f_{1}^{\otimes k};r_{k}=s_{k};r_{k};f_{k}=Id_{A_{k}};f_{k}=f_{k}
ie.
Equation

12
is verified. Suppose now that
Equation

12
is verified. We know from
Proposition

45
that we have:

and thus
f_{n+p};\Delta_{n,p}=\binom{n+p}{n}f_{n+p};s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p};s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}

=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}\sigma;r_{n}\otimes r_{p}=\frac{1}{n!p!}s_{n+p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}\sigma;r_{n}\otimes r_{p}

=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}s_{n+p};\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}s_{n+p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}

=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}

But we also have that

s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p}=s_{n+p};(r_{n};s_{n})\otimes(r_{p};s_{p})=s_{n+p};(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma)\otimes(\frac{1}{p!}\underset{\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}}{\sum}\tau)

=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}s_{n+p};\sigma\otimes\tau=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}s_{n+p}=\frac{1}{n!p!}(n!p!)s_{n+p}=s_{n+p}

Thus
f_{n+p};\Delta_{n,p}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n}\otimes r_{p}

=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p};(s_{n};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n})\otimes(s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes p};r_{p})=\Delta_{n,p};f_{n}\otimes f_{p}
ie.
Equation

13
is verified. Suppose now that
Equation

13
is verified. We then have
s_{k};f_{1}^{\otimes k}=f_{k};s_{k}
for every
2\leq k\leq n
by induction:
\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{1,1};f_{1}\otimes f_{1}=\frac{1}{2}f_{2};\Delta_{1,1}=f_{2};(\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{1,1})=f_{2};s_{2}
. Now suppose that it is true for some
2\leq k\leq n-1
, we then have
s_{k+1};f_{1}^{\otimes(k+1)}=\frac{1}{k+1}\Delta_{k,1};s_{k}\otimes 1_{A_{1}};f_{1}^{\otimes(k+1)}=\frac{1}{k+1}\Delta_{k,1};(s_{k};f_{1}^{\otimes k})\otimes f_{1}=\frac{1}{k+1}\Delta_{k,1};(f_{k};s_{k})\otimes f_{1}=\frac{1}{k+1}\Delta_{k,1};f_{k}\otimes f_{1};s_{k}\otimes 1_{B_{1}}=\frac{1}{k+1}f_{k+1};\Delta_{k,1};s_{k}\otimes 1_{B_{1}}=f_{k+1};\frac{1}{k+1}\Delta_{k,1};s_{k}\otimes 1_{B_{1}}=f_{k+1};s_{k+1}
. We thus have
s_{k};f_{1}^{\otimes k};r_{k}=f_{k};s_{k};r_{k}=f_{k};1_{A_{k}}=f_{k}
ie.

12
is verified. Suppose now that
