and thus
\nabla_{n,p};f_{n+p}=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p};f_{n+p}=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p};s_{n+p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}

=\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S_{n+p}}}{\sum}s_{n}\otimes s_{p};\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}=\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S_{n+p}}}{\sum}s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};\sigma;r_{n+p}

=\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S_{n+p}}}{\sum}s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}=\frac{1}{(n+p)!}(n+p)!s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n+p}

But we also have that
r_{n}\otimes r_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}=(r_{n};s_{n})\otimes(r_{p};s_{p});r_{n+p}=(\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma)\otimes(\frac{1}{p!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}}{\sum}\tau);r_{n+p}

=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}\sigma\otimes\tau;r_{n+p}=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}r_{n+p}=\frac{1}{n!p!}(n!p!)r_{n+p}=r_{n+p}

Thus
\nabla_{n,p};f_{n+p}=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes(n+p)};r_{n}\otimes r_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}

=s_{n}\otimes s_{p};f_{1}^{\otimes n}\otimes f_{1}^{\otimes p};r_{n}\otimes r_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}=f_{n}\otimes f_{p};s_{n}\otimes s_{p};r_{n+p}=f_{n}\otimes f_{p};\nabla_{n,p}

ie.
Equation

11
is verified.
∎

Proposition

49
follows.

Proposition 51
.

Let
(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}
,
(B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
be two permutation splittings. Then
(f_{n}:A_{n}\rightarrow B_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is an isomorphism of permutation splittings iff
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings and
f_{1}
is an isomorphism.

Proof.

Suppose that
f_{1}
is an isomorphism and that
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings. Then
f_{n}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}
. We show that every
f_{n}
is an isomorphism and that
f_{n}^{-1}=s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}
. We have
f_{n};s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B};s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}

=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}=s_{n}^{A};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes n};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}=s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}=s_{n}^{A};r_{n}^{A}=Id_{A_{n}}
. Moreover,
s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A};f_{n}=s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A};s_{n}^{A};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}

=s_{n}^{B};\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma;(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{B}=s_{n}^{B};r_{n}^{B}=Id_{B_{n}}
.

We now verify that
(f_{n}^{-1})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings. We must show that

f_{n}^{-1}=s_{n}^{B};(f_{1}^{-1})^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{A}
, but it is exactly how we defined
f_{n}^{-1}
. So, this equation is verified and
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is an isomorphism of permutation splittings.
∎

10
Unicities of algebraic structures on a family of symmetric powers

In this section, we show that if a graded object can be equipped with an algebraic structure of permutations splitting or of binomial graded bimonoid, then this algebraic structure is unique up to isomorphism. In fact, we have a bit more as the algebraic structure, up to isomorphism, depends only on the isomorphism class of the first object.

Proposition 52
.

Let
P_{1}=((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n}^{1})_{n\geq 2},(s_{n}^{1})_{n\geq 2})
and
P_{2}=((A_{n})_{n\geq 2},(r_{n}^{2})_{n\geq 2},(s_{n}^{2})_{n\geq 2})
be two permutation splittings with the same underlying graded object. Then
P_{1}
and
P_{2}
are isomorphic as permutation splittings.

Proof.

Write
f_{1}=Id_{A_{1}}
and
f_{n}=s_{n}^{1};r_{n}^{2}
for every
n\geq 2
. Then
f_{1}
is an isomorphism. We must verify that
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is a morphism of permutation splittings ie. show that
s_{n}^{1};f_{1}^{\otimes n};r_{n}^{2}=f_{n}
. It is immediate as
f_{n}=s_{n}^{1};r_{n}^{2}
by definition and
f_{1}=Id_{A_{1}}
.
(f_{n})_{n\geq 1}
is thus an isomorphism of permutation splittings by
Proposition

51
.
∎

Proposition 53
.

Let
P_{1}=((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n}^{1})_{n\geq 1},(s_{n}^{1})_{n\geq 2})
and
P_{2}=((B_{n})_{n\geq 1},(r_{n}^{2})_{n\geq 2},(s_{n}^{2})_{n\geq 2})
be two permutation splittings such that
A_{1}\cong B_{1}
. Then
P_{1}
and
P_{2}
are isomorphic as permutation splittings.

Proof.

Let
\phi_{1}:A_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}
be an isomorphism.
F_{2}(P_{1})
and
F_{2}(P_{2})
are then two permutation splittings in the reduced category of permutation splittings. Morphisms in the reduced category of permutation splittings are just morphisms between the first underlying objects, thus
\phi_{1}
is an isomorphism from
F_{2}(P_{1})
to
F_{2}(P_{2})
. Thus
F_{2}^{-1}(\phi_{1})
is an isomorphism from
P_{1}
to
P_{2}
in the category of permutation splittings.
∎

Proposition 54
.

Let
B_{1}=((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}^{1})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}^{1})_{n,p\geq 1})

and
B_{2}=((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}^{2})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}^{2})_{n,p\geq 1})
be two binomial graded bimonoids with the same underlying graded object. Then
B_{1}
and
B_{2}
are isomorphic as binomial graded bimonoids.

Proof.

F_{1}
preserves the underlying graded objects, thus
F_{1}(B_{1})
and
F_{1}(B_{2})
are two permutation splittings with the same underlying graded object. Therefore, they are isomorphic as permutation splittings by
Proposition

52
. By applying
G_{1}=F_{1}^{-1}
, we obtain that
B_{1}
and
B_{2}
are isomorphic as binomial graded bimonoids.
∎

Proposition 55
.

Let
B=((A_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}^{1})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}^{1})_{n,p\geq 1})
and
B^{\prime}=((B_{n})_{n\geq 1},(\nabla_{n,p}^{2})_{n,p\geq 1},(\Delta_{n,p}^{2})_{n,p\geq 1})
be two binomial graded bimonoids such that
A_{1}\cong B_{1}
. Then
B
and
B^{\prime}
are isomorphic as binomial graded bimonoids.

Proof.

F_{1}(B)
and
F_{1}(B^{\prime})
are two permutation splittings with the same underlying graded objects and such that
A_{1}\cong B_{1}
. It follows from
Proposition

53
that
F_{1}(B)
and
F_{1}(B^{\prime})
are isomorphic as permutation splittings. By applying
F_{1}^{-1}
,
B
and
B^{\prime}
are thus isomorphic binomial graded bimonoids.
∎

11
Base change for symmetric monoidal
k
-linear categories

In this section,
k
will designate a commutative semi-ring. Remember that if
r
is another semi-ring, then we say that it is a
k
-algebra if it is equipped with a semi-ring morphism
\rho:k\rightarrow Z(r)
where
Z(r)
is the center of
r
ie. a map which preserves sums, products, additive and multiplicative units. Every
k
-algebra is a
k
-module.

Proposition 56
.

In a symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
, for every object
A
, the hom-set
\mathcal{C}[A,A]
is a
k
-algebra. If
A=I
, then
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
is a commutative
k
-algebra. For every objects
A,B
, the hom-set
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is a
(\mathcal{C}[A,A],\mathcal{C}[B,B])
-bimodule.

Proof.

The structure of
k
-algebra on
\mathcal{C}[A,A]
is obtained by taking the product equal to the composition, the multiplicative unit is then
1_{A}
, the addition is the addition given on any hom-set and the composition is distributive over the addition by definition of a symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category. It is also given by the definition that
0;f=f;0=0
. We thus know that
\mathcal{C}[A,A]
is a semi-ring. The structure of
k
-algebra is given by the map
\rho:k\rightarrow Z(\mathcal{C}[A,A])
which sends
\lambda
to
\lambda.1_{A}
.

Therefore
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
is a
k
-algebra by taking
A=I
. The more difficult fact is that it is a commutative one. It is a consequence of Proposition 6.1 in
[
34
]
: in any monoidal category the composition in
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
is commutative ie.
f;g=g;f
if
f,g\in\mathcal{C}[I,I]
, moreover, we also have
f;g=f\otimes g
(under our assumption of strict monoidality, if one wishes to work with the coherences, then we must put a unitor before and after the tensor product) and thus
g\otimes f=f\otimes g
if
f,g\in\mathcal{C}[I,I]
.

The fact that
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is a
(\mathcal{C}[A,A],\mathcal{C}[B,B])
-bimodule is not more difficult than the fact that
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is a
k
-algebra and is in the same way a direct consequence of the definition of symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category.
∎

Proposition 57
.

If
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category where
k
is an algebra over a commutative semi-ring
r
, then
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
r
-linear category.

Proof.

Denote by
\rho:r\rightarrow k
the semi-ring morphism which makes
k
a
r
-algebra. Then every hom-set
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is a
r
-module by defining
\lambda.f:=\rho(\lambda).f
. It is then an easy consequence of the definitions that
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
r
-linear category.
∎

Corollary 58
.

Every symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is a symmetric monoidal
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
-linear category.

Proof.

We already know that
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is an additive commutative monoid by definition of a symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category.

The action of
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
on
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is given for
\lambda\in\mathcal{C}[I,I]
and
f\in\mathcal{C}[A,B]
by
\lambda\otimes f:A\rightarrow B
. The properties of the action which makes
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
a
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
-module are then direct consequences of the definition of a symmetric monoidal
k
-linear category and we finally obtain that
\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
-linear category.
∎

12
Examples

In this section, we give two examples of symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear categories with symmetric powers. We compute binomial graded bimonoids from permutation splittings in the two cases.

Definition 59
.

A symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category
\mathcal{C}
is additively idempotent if, for every morphism
f:A\rightarrow B
, we have that
f+f=f
.

Definition 60
.

\mathbb{B}
is the semi-ring whose underlying set is
\{0,1\}
and such that
1+1=1
.

Proposition 61
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category. These conditions are equivalent:

•

\mathcal{C}
is additively idempotent

•

\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{B}
-linear

•

\mathcal{C}[I,I]
(with its canonical structure of semi-ring from
Proposition

56
) is a
\mathbb{B}
-algebra

If any of these conditions is verified, then
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear.

Proof.

If
\mathcal{C}
is additively idempotent, then
\mathcal{C}[A,B]
is a
\mathbb{B}
-module by defining
0.f=0
and
1.f=f
. The main reason why it works is because
(1+1).f=1.f=f=f+f=1.f+1.f
.
\mathcal{C}
is then
\mathbb{B}
-linear. If
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{B}
-linear, then
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
is a
\mathbb{B}
-algebra thanks to
Proposition

56
. If
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
is a
\mathbb{B}
-algebra, then it is commutative, we know from
Corollary

58
that
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathcal{C}[I,I]
-linear and then from
Proposition

57
that
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{B}
-linear. If
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{B}
-linear, we then have for every
f:A\rightarrow B
that
f=1.f=(1+1).f=(1.f)+(1.f)=f+f
ie.
\mathcal{C}
is additively idempotent.

Moreover,
\mathbb{B}
is a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-algebra by defining
0.x=0
and
r.x=x
if
r\neq 0
, for every
r\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
and
x\in\mathbb{B}
. The main reason why it works is that the multiplication and the addition are idempotent in
\mathbb{B}
and thus for instance if
r,r^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}
, then
(r.r^{\prime}).x=x=r.x=r.(r^{\prime}.x)
and
(r+r^{\prime}).x=x=x+x=r.x+r^{\prime}.x
. It follows that if any of these conditions is verified, then
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{B}
-linear and thanks to
Proposition

57
,
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear.
∎

Example 62
.

The category
\mathbf{Rel}
of sets and relations is a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{N}
-linear category with tensor product the cartesian product, monoidal unit a one-element set, zero morphism the empty relation, and the sum of morphisms given by the union of relations. It is a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category since it is additively idempotent. Moreover,
Rel[I,I]
is isomorphic to
\mathbb{B}=\{0,1\}
.

Example 63
.

The category
\mathbf{Mod}_{R}
of modules over a commutative
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-algebra
R
is a symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category.

We now compute binomial graded bimonoids in these two categories, starting with a permutation splitting.

In
\mathbf{Rel}
, we obtain a permutation splitting for every set
X
by defining for every
n\geq 2
,
r_{n}:X^{\times n}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{n}(X)
by
r_{n}=\{((x_{1},...,x_{n}),[x_{1},...,x_{n}]),x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X\}
and
s_{n}:\mathcal{M}_{n}(X)\rightarrow X^{\times n}
by

s_{n}=\{(([x_{1},...,x_{n}],(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)})),x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\}
.

Indeed, we obtain that
r_{n};s_{n}=\{((x_{1},...,x_{n}),(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)}),x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\}

=\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\bigcup}\{((x_{1},...,x_{n}),(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)}),x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X\}

=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\bigcup}\{((x_{1},...,x_{n}),(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)}),x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X\}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\bigcup}\sigma

and that
s_{n};r_{n}=\{[x_{1},...,x_{n}],[x_{1},...,x_{n}],x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X\}=1_{\mathcal{M}_{n}(X)}
.

We now apply
G_{1}
to this permutation splitting and thus define

\displaystyle\nabla_{n,p}

\displaystyle=s_{n}\times s_{p};r_{n+p}

\displaystyle=\{(([x_{1},...,x_{n}],(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)})),x_{1},...,x_{n}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\}\times\{(([y_{1},...,y_{p}],(y_{\tau(1)},...,y_{\tau(p)})),y_{1},...,y_{p}\in X,\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\};

\displaystyle\{((w_{1},...,w_{n+p}),[w_{1},...,w_{n+p}]),w_{1},...,w_{n+p}\in X\}

\displaystyle=\{(([x_{1},...,x_{n}],[y_{1},...,y_{p}]),((x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)},y_{\tau(1)},...,y_{\tau(p)}))),x_{1},...,x_{n},y_{1},...,y_{p}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\};

\displaystyle\{((w_{1},...,w_{n+p}),[w_{1},...,w_{n+p}]),w_{1},...,w_{n+p}\in X\}

\displaystyle=\{(([x_{1},...,x_{n}],[y_{1},...,y_{p}]),[x_{1},...,x_{n},y_{1},...,y_{p}]),x_{1},...,x_{n},y_{1},...,y_{n+p}\in X\}

In words:
\nabla_{n,p}
relates a bag of
n
elements and a bag of
p
elements to the bag of all these
n+p
elements.

\displaystyle\Delta_{n,p}

\displaystyle=\binom{n}{n+p}s_{n+p};r_{n}\times r_{p}=s_{n+p};r_{n}\times r_{p}

\displaystyle=\{([x_{1},...,x_{n+p}],(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n+p)})),x_{1},...,x_{n+p}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}\};

\displaystyle\{((y_{1},...,y_{n}),[y_{1},...,y_{n}]),y_{1},...,y_{n}\in X\}\times\{((w_{1},...,w_{p}),[w_{1},...,w_{p}]),w_{1},...,w_{p}\in X\}

\displaystyle=\{([x_{1},...,x_{n+p}],(x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n+p)})),x_{1},...,x_{n+p}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}\};

\displaystyle\{((y_{1},...,y_{n},w_{1},...,w_{p}),([y_{1},...,y_{n}],[w_{1},...,w_{p}])),y_{1},...,y_{n},w_{1},...,w_{p}\in X\}

\displaystyle=\{([x_{1},...,x_{n+p}],([x_{\sigma(1)},...,x_{\sigma(n)}],[x_{\sigma(n+1)},...,x_{\sigma(n+p)}])),x_{1},...,x_{n+p}\in X,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}\}

In words:
\Delta_{n,p}
relates a bag of
n+p
elements to all the pairs of a bag of
n
elements and a bag of
p
elements obtained by dividing the bag of
n+p
elements into two bags.

By the properties of
G_{1}
for any symmetric monoidal
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-linear category, we know that we have thus defined a binomial graded bimonoid.

Let
R
be a commutative semi-ring which is a
\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
-algebra. In
\mathbf{Mod}_{R}
, we obtain a permutation splitting for every module
M
by defining for every
n\geq 2
,
r_{n}^{(1)}:M^{\otimes n}\rightarrow S^{n}(M)
as the unique linear map from
M^{\otimes n}
to
S^{n}(M)
such that
r_{n}^{(1)}(x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n})=x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}
and
s_{n}^{(1)}:S^{n}(M)\rightarrow M^{\otimes n}
as the unique linear map from
S^{n}(M)
to
M^{\otimes n}
such that
s_{n}(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{x}x_{n})=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}
.

Indeed, we obtain that
(r_{n}^{(1)};s_{n}^{(1)})(x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n})=s_{n}(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n})=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}
, thus
r_{n}^{(1)};s_{n}^{(1)}=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}\sigma
and that
(s_{n}^{(1)};r_{n}^{(1)})(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n})=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}=x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}
, thus
r_{n}^{(1)};s_{n}^{(1)}=1_{S^{n}(M)}
.

We now apply
G^{1}
to this permutation splitting and thus define
\nabla_{n,p}^{(1)}=s_{n}^{(1)}\otimes s_{p}^{(1)};r_{n+p}^{(1)}
and
\Delta_{n,p}^{(1)}=\binom{n+p}{n}s_{n+p}^{(1)};r_{n}^{(1)}\otimes r_{p}^{(1)}
.

We compute that

\displaystyle\nabla_{n,p}^{(1)}((x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n})\otimes(y_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}y_{p}))

\displaystyle=r_{n+p}^{(1)}\bigg(\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}\otimes y_{\tau(1)}\otimes...\otimes y_{\tau(p)}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)}\otimes_{s}y_{\tau(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes y_{\tau(p)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!p!}(n!p!)x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)}\otimes_{s}y_{\tau(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes y_{\tau(p)}

\displaystyle=x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}\otimes_{s}y_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes y_{p}

and that (see the footnote for the details of the last steps)
1
1

1

Notice that given
x_{1},...,x_{n+p}\in M
, for every
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
the value of
x_{\tau(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\tau(n)}
is the same. It thus makes sense to define
x_{A}:=x_{a_{1}}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{a_{n}}
for any subset
A=\{a_{1},...,a_{n}\}
of
n
elements of [1,n+p]. Given such a subset
A
, there are exactly
n!p!
permutations
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}
such that
A=\{\sigma(1),...,\sigma(n)\}
and
[1,n+p]\backslash A=\{\sigma(n+1),...,\sigma(n+p)\}
. Indeed, we know that
1,...,n
must be sent each one to some value in
A
, there are
n!
ways to do that and
n+1,...,n+p
must be sent each one to some value in
[1,n+p]\backslash A
, there are
p!
ways to do that. Moreover, given two distinct such subsets
A,B
of
n
elements of
[1,n+p]
, the two sets of
n!p!
permutations associated respectively to
A
and to
B
are disjoints because these permutations are respectively such that
\{\sigma(1),...,\sigma(n)\}=A
or such that
\{\sigma(1),...,\sigma(n)\}=B
. We thus have shown that
\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}
is partitionned into
\binom{n+p}{n}
sets of
n!p!
permutations, each of this set being the set
S(A)
of permutations
\sigma
such that
\{\sigma(1),...,\sigma(n)\}=A
for some subset
A
of
n
elements of
[1,n+p]
.

\displaystyle\Delta_{n,p}^{(1)}(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n+p})

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}(r_{n}^{(1)}\otimes r_{p}^{(1)})\bigg(\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n+p)}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}(x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)})\otimes(x_{\sigma(n+1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n+p)})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}\underset{\sigma\in S(A)}{\sum}(x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)})\otimes(x_{\sigma(n+1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n+p)})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}\underset{\sigma\in S(A)}{\sum}x_{A}\otimes x_{[1,...,n+p]\backslash A}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}(n!p!)x_{A}\otimes x_{[1,...,n+p]\backslash A}

\displaystyle=\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}x_{A}\otimes x_{[1,...,n+p]\backslash A}

We now start with another permutation splitting in
\mathbf{Mod}_{R}
. For every
n\geq 2
, we define
r_{n}^{(2)}:M^{\otimes n}\rightarrow S^{n}(M)
by
r_{n}^{(2)}(x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n})=\frac{1}{n!}x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}
and
s_{n}^{(2)}:S^{n}(M)\rightarrow M^{\otimes n}
by
s_{n}^{(2)}(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n})=\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...x_{\sigma(n)}
. We compute

\displaystyle\nabla_{n,p}^{(2)}((x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n})\otimes(y_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}y_{p}))

\displaystyle=r_{n+p}^{(2)}\bigg(\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}\otimes y_{\tau(1)}\otimes...\otimes y_{\tau(p)}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(n+p)!}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p}\end{subarray}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)}\otimes_{s}y_{\tau(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes y_{\tau(p)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(n+p)!}(n!p!)x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}\otimes_{s}y_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes y_{p}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\binom{n+p}{n}}x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n}\otimes_{s}y_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes y_{p}

and

\displaystyle\Delta_{n,p}^{(2)}(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n+p})

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}(r_{n}^{(2)}\otimes r_{p}^{(2)})\bigg(\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes...\otimes x_{\sigma(n+p)}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+p}}{\sum}(x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)})\otimes(x_{\sigma(n+1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n+p)})

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}\underset{\sigma\in S(A)}{\sum}(x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)})\otimes(x_{\sigma(n+1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n+p)})

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}\underset{\sigma\in S(A)}{\sum}x_{A}\otimes x_{[1,...,n+p]\backslash A}

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}\frac{1}{n!p!}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}(n!p!)x_{A}\otimes x_{[1,...,n+p]\backslash A}

\displaystyle=\binom{n+p}{n}\underset{A\in\mathcal{P}_{n}([1,n+p])}{\sum}x_{A}\otimes x_{[1,...,n+p]\backslash A}

We now replace the symmetric powers with the divided powers. We define
r_{n}^{(3)}:M^{\otimes n}\rightarrow\Gamma^{n}(M)
by
r_{n}^{(3)}(x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n})=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n}
and
s_{n}^{(3)}:\Gamma^{n}(M)\rightarrow M^{\otimes n}
is the subspace inclusion.

\nabla_{n,p}^{(3)}
is then the symmetrization
r_{n}^{(3)}
applied to an element of
\Gamma^{n}(M)\otimes\Gamma^{p}(M)
as an element of
M^{\otimes(n+p)}
whereas
\Delta_{n,p}^{(3)}
is obtained by applying
\binom{n+p}{n}r_{n}^{(3)}\otimes r_{p}^{(3)}
to an element of
\Gamma^{n+p}(M)
as an element of
M^{\otimes(n+p)}
.

We can also define
r_{n}^{(4)}:M^{\otimes n}\rightarrow\Gamma^{n}(M)
by
r_{n}^{(4)}(x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n})=\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{1}\otimes...\otimes x_{n}
and
s_{n}^{(4)}:\Gamma^{n}(M)\rightarrow M^{\otimes n}
by
\frac{1}{n!}
times the inclusion. We now obtain that
\nabla_{n,p}^{(4)}=\binom{n+p}{n}\nabla_{n,p}^{(3)}
and
\Delta_{n,p}^{(4)}=\frac{1}{\binom{n+p}{n}}\Delta_{n,p}^{(3)}
.

Of course, by
Proposition

54
,
(S^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(1)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(1)}))
,
(S^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(2)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(2)}))
,
(\Gamma^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(3)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(3)}))

and
(\Gamma^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(4)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(4)}))
are all isomorphic binomial graded bialgebras. An isomorphism from

(S^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(1)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(1)}))

to
(S^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(2)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(2)}))
is given by
\frac{1}{n!}Id_{S^{n}(M)}
, an isomorphism from

(\Gamma^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(3)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(3)}))

to
(\Gamma^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(4)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(4)}))
is given by
(n!)Id_{\Gamma^{n}(M)}
and an isomorphism from

(S^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(1)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(1)}))

to
(\Gamma^{n}(M),(\nabla_{n,p}^{(3)}),(\Delta_{n,p}^{(3)}))
is given by
\phi^{n}:S^{n}(M)\rightarrow\Gamma^{n}(N)
defined by
\phi^{n}(x_{1}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{n})=\frac{1}{n!}\underset{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}{\sum}x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes_{s}...\otimes_{s}x_{\sigma(n)}
.
